Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation is a colony management and survival strategy game developed and published by Suncrash that takes familiar settlement-building mechanics and places them inside a world devastated by supernatural catastrophe. Instead of rebuilding civilization after disease, war, or environmental collapse, players are forced to survive in a reality where demonic forces have invaded Earth and reduced humanity to scattered pockets of survivors. The result is a game that blends colony simulation, tactical combat, crafting systems, and survival pressure into a dark and engaging experience built around persistence against overwhelming odds.

The premise immediately gives the game a unique identity. Humanity stands on the edge of extinction after infernal creatures tear through civilization, leaving chaos behind. A small band of survivors manages to escape destruction and establish a hidden refuge away from immediate danger. From that fragile beginning, players slowly transform a desperate shelter into a functioning community capable of surviving increasingly dangerous threats. The journey is not simply about expansion. It is about enduring a hostile world that constantly pushes back.

Base construction forms the core of progression. Resources gathered from dangerous expeditions fuel every aspect of growth. Players build farms, workshops, living spaces, storage facilities, and defensive structures while balancing survival needs against long-term development. Every decision carries consequences because resources remain limited and threats continue escalating. Expanding too aggressively can create vulnerabilities, while moving too cautiously may leave the colony unable to withstand future dangers.

Managing survivors becomes equally important. Each individual contributes through assigned responsibilities that help maintain efficiency throughout the settlement. Gathering materials, farming food, crafting supplies, researching technologies, and defending the colony all compete for limited manpower. Effective organization becomes essential because poor planning creates shortages that can quickly spiral into larger problems. The colony succeeds only when multiple systems work together efficiently.

One of the strongest aspects of Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation comes from how naturally survival systems interact with supernatural pressure. Resource management alone would create challenge, but demonic enemies introduce constant danger that prevents players from becoming too comfortable. Defensive preparation matters because attacks can arrive unexpectedly, forcing players to maintain combat readiness alongside economic development. The game consistently balances growth against survival in a way that keeps tension high.

Combat adds another layer of strategy through squad-based engagements that emphasize preparation and positioning. Players control groups of survivors during encounters while balancing equipment choices and tactical decisions under pressure. Battles reward planning rather than simple aggression. Strong equipment helps, but survival often depends more heavily on intelligent positioning and understanding individual survivor strengths.

The world outside the colony provides another major source of engagement. Exploration missions send survivors into dangerous territory filled with opportunities and risks. Valuable resources, hidden locations, and additional survivors wait beyond the safety of the settlement, but dangerous encounters can easily turn expeditions into disasters. Every mission creates meaningful decisions regarding risk management. Valuable supplies may justify danger, but losing experienced survivors can cripple progress significantly.

Progression systems further strengthen long-term investment. Research unlocks stronger technology, improved infrastructure, and advanced survival options that gradually expand player capabilities. One of the more interesting aspects comes from how the game embraces supernatural themes fully. Instead of merely fighting dark forces, players eventually gain opportunities to study and utilize occult knowledge themselves. This unusual design choice creates interesting strategic possibilities while reinforcing the game's darker atmosphere.

Character development contributes additional depth. Survivors gradually improve through experience and specialization, becoming more efficient in different roles over time. Assigning responsibilities based on strengths creates opportunities for optimization while strengthening attachment to individual colony members. Success begins feeling tied not only to infrastructure but also to maintaining a capable and balanced population.

Visually, the game favors function over spectacle. The isometric presentation keeps important information readable while supporting the bleak atmosphere effectively. Environmental design communicates desperation without becoming visually overwhelming. The focus remains squarely on systems and strategy rather than graphical complexity, which suits the genre well.

The game's complexity naturally creates challenges of its own. As settlements grow larger, managing priorities becomes increasingly demanding. Balancing production chains, survivor assignments, research progression, and defensive preparation simultaneously can become overwhelming during later stages. Some players may find the growing responsibility stressful, but strategy fans will likely appreciate the depth that emerges from those interconnected systems.

What ultimately makes Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation stand apart is how effectively it merges multiple ideas together. Colony building, survival management, exploration, crafting, combat, and supernatural themes all support one another naturally. The game never feels like disconnected mechanics forced together. Instead, each system strengthens the larger experience.

Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation succeeds because it transforms survival into a constant balancing act between ambition and caution. Growth feels rewarding because every improvement requires careful planning and resilience. Surviving one disaster simply prepares players for the next challenge waiting beyond the colony walls.

Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation delivers a rewarding combination of settlement management, survival strategy, and supernatural tension that creates a compelling experience filled with meaningful decisions and long-term progression.

tl;dr: good base building, horrible, annoying, boring combat.

Let's get combat out of the way first. There are two kinds of combat: auto-combat and manual. In scavenging missions you can choose to auto-resolve or manage combat manually. In rescue missions (which is how you get new survivors; you rescue them from demons), story missions, support missions (when you are called to support other colonies) and when enemies attack your base you only have the option to fight manually. In a manual fight you start with all your survivors in one end of the map and the map is covered in the Fog of War so you have to explore a bit to find an objective, which is either some scavenging point or a caged survivor. If you don't encounter any enemies while searching for objectives, they will attack you anyway when you start scavenging or trying to free the caged survivor, because you make noise while at it (the chance for that is reduced by Stealth but for my survivors it never makes much of a difference). Combat starts the moment enemies are in range: they start shooting you or they rush you in close combat. Your survivors can also fight in melee or shoot, depending on their equipped weapons, but each survivor gets only one weapon slot so you can't have a guy armed with a knife and a bow at the same time, say, which is a very odd choice. If that's supposed to give some tactical depth to combat, it's obscured by the fact that survivors will only attack enemies who are in range and will not move to get closer to enemies, even if those enemies are actively attacking them, like, personally. So if you don't order a survivor to attack a ranged enemy that's shooting her she just stands there and takes it like a man until she's dead, Jim. That means you have to pause combat all the time and direct every survivor carefully or else they are knocked out and start bleeding to death. While a survivor is bleeding, another one can go and stabilise them, but of course they are a sitting duck while doing so. Worst, it's very hard to click on the downed survivor in the middle of a melee with enemies and friends all around them so I've lost a few survivors because I couldn't click on them to start stabilising them in time.

Combat is generally stacked against you until you can start producing high-end armour with lots of "Armour" stat (i.e. damage absorption) otherwise the "Evasion" that ordinary armour gives you is all but useless in practice, enemies will hit you and kill you like you're naked anyway. So it's like D&D Armour Class but worse because it's always low and forget about taking. Even with high-end armour and healing items I still get survivors maimed or dying in every rescue mission which basically defeats the whole purpose of a rescue mission. Why lose my best fighters to save a low-level guy with random, possibly useless, traits?

Survivors have equipment and abilities they can use in the middle of combat but honestly, most of them are not worth the trouble. Healing items, even the ones that say they heal "100%", don't. Mass healing abilities heal like 5-10% of damage in each survivor they reach if that. It doesn't matter because enemies do many times more damage than you ever have time to heal. Magical items you can take in battle feel completely useless and I haven't even bothered. There are three equipment slots in each survivor, for a main weapon, armour and misc item, but the misc item can be a shield (which usually only increases Evasion) or a healing item and I really can't tell why I should give up a shield or healing slot to take with me an item that ... hexes the enemy and the survivor using it? For a 10% Accuracy debuff?

Overall, manual combat is frustrating, boring, annoying and I don't want to do it but there's no way around it, so I just grind my teeth and get on with it, save scumming if I have to. 

When combat is over, whether it was manual or auto-resolved you get a screen that shows you how much (permanent) damage your survivors sustained (they can also get injuries which take time to heal in the Infirmary) and what enemies they killed, plus the loot collected if any.

Now, here's the thing. It is very obvious, when you look at that screen, that my survivors fare a lot better in auto-resolved battles than when I manually resolve combat. Maybe that's a skill issue but in that case, where's the "Easy" mode? Well, there isn't any. Or maybe that *is* the easy mode and it doesn't get any harder because then you'd throw the controller? But honestly it looks like the same survivors can survive multiple rounds with minimal damage against the same level of enemy in auto-resolve that kill them all in manual combat and that's just unbalanced.

Bottom line: for me (this is my review) combat really, really sucks and the reason seems to be all the micromanagement that is caused by the choice of real-time-with-pause. I would probably enjoy it a lot more if it were simply turn-based.

Now, the base building. Well that's actually not bad at all and it's the only reason I have as much time as I do in the game. There are endless crafting trees to unlock and it's always a bit confusing what you have to unlock to produce which material to allow you to build what *other* material so you can build some item or building you want, but that's OK, it's part of discovering the game. There are both mundane and occult crafting trees and you can cast rituals to make your survivors heal faster, work faster, scout better etc, but those are tbh a bit lackluster and I'd like to see more diversity and more powerful rituals to better match the effort you have to put into creating the various holy/unholy buildings that enable them.

Materials for crafting and building come form the initial camp. You can immediately collect wood, stone, clay and "Scrap" from scavenging piles,  but you need more advanced buildings for metal and other minerals that let you craft more advanced items. You have to be careful not to run out of trees because then you're out of wood although you can always plant trees and wait for them to grow. You can also scavenge materials which is where you get the auto-resolve battles, and you can also trade or get some materials in events and from other survivor colonies you encounter on the map while scavenging or going after story missions. Trading is a bit meh, everything is always overpriced and you pay ten times the "scrap" you make for selling the same item. So just like ebay. 

There is an outpost mechanic that lets you mine resources from the map, but I haven't used it much until now because I still have all the resources I need in the base camp.

There are special research materials that you need in order to progress your research trees which are a very transparent ploy to force you to move out of your base and explore/scavenge. Not a great choice but I kind of liked the scavenging mechanic, especially since you can auto-resolve battles, so it doesn't feel too oppressive to me.

Survivors are all a bit samey-samey and they take forever to level up. There is a story but it's pretty basic. At first it feels a little different-for-the-sake-of-different that you're fighting demons rather than zombies, but I guess that opens up the various occult options in the skill and build/craft trees so OK.

Overall, I would like to keep playing but I'm not sure I want to, because of the miserable and boring combat. As usual I'm sorry I can't give a thumbs-horizontal, so I have to give a thumbs down just because of the combat.

The biggest problem with this game is there is a number of much better colony sims. This game just doesn't feel very fun. It's tedious and mechanically shallow. Combat isn't fun, colony management isn't fun, and it feels just barely better than a web game. The building is also overly simplistic, there's no freeform building. You build pre-designed structures that face forward. The flat design of the structures and backgrounds contrasts heavily with the 3D design of the characters. The game isn't "terrible" if you get it for cheap and just want to play a 'different' colony sim than the ones you already have, but I'd recommend literally almost any other colony sim over this. 

Just get Rimworld, Stranded: Alien Dawn, Ratopia, Craft The World, Oxygen Not Included, Mind Over Magic, Cult of the Lamb, Palworld, or really any other colony sim or game with colony sim mechanics instead. If you can get this cheap, it's not terrible if you want to play a simple colony sim. But just keep low expectations going in.

Judgment — це стратегія про виживання в постапокаліпсисі, яка могла б стати цікавою, але, на жаль, не стала. Розробники взяли непогану концепцію і... ну, скажімо так, не довели до розуму.

Що зачепило:
• Атмосфера постапоку дійсно відчувається
• Дерево технологій опрацьовано гідно
• Ідея керування групою виживших у зруйнованому світі під час вторгнення демонів звучить спокусливо

А тепер про те, чому гра розчаровує:
1. Бій перетворився на м'ясиво Система укриттів для галочки, тактики ніякої — просто тупо клікаєш по ворогах і чекаєш, коли вони помруть. Ні напруження, ні роздумів про позиціонування. Бійка деградує у звичайну м'ясорубку.

2. Випадкові події? Які події? Після перших 2-3 годин розумієш, що "випадковості" у грі повторюються із завидною регулярністю. Той же набір ситуацій крутиться по колу — нудьга смертельна.

3. Візуал часів флеш-ігор Графіка та анімації виглядають так, ніби їх робили у 2005 році. Причому не кращі зразки того часу. Персонажі рухаються як дерев'яні ляльки.
4. Торгівля і дипломатія для галочки Торгові націнки космічні. А "дипломатія" зводиться до двох варіантів: допоможи відбитися або дай ресурсів. Вся взаємодія з іншими поселеннями вміщується у пару кліків.

5. Геймплей з'їжджає у рутину Перші години ще цікаво, але потім перетворюється на одноманітний ґрінд. Досліджуєш карту на автопілоті, збираєш ресурси, будуєш споруди — і так до нескінченності.

Вердикт: 4/10 Judgment міг би бути непоганою грою для шанувальників жанру, якби не купа недоробок. У поточному стані це швидше демка цікавої концепції, ніж повноцінна гра. Купувати варто тільки на великій знижці і тільки якщо зовсім нічого грати.

Spiel:
Ich habe mittlerweile knapp 60 Stunden in "Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation" investiert und bin absolut begeistert. Das Spiel vereint auf geniale Weise Strategie, Simulation und Survival-Elemente und bietet dabei eine fesselnde und tiefgründige Spielerfahrung.

Atmosphäre:
Die Atmosphäre des Spiels ist packend und düster, während man versucht, eine kleine Gruppe von Überlebenden durch eine von Dämonen heimgesuchte Welt zu führen.

Balance und Strategie:
Die Balance zwischen Ressourcenmanagement, Basisbau und taktischen Kämpfen sorgt für durchgehende Spannung und strategische Herausforderungen.

Charakterentwicklung:
Die Charakterentwicklung ist sehr gut umgesetzt. Jeder Überlebende hat eigene Fähigkeiten und Persönlichkeiten, was das Spiel sehr dynamisch und abwechslungsreich macht.

Kämpfe:
Die Kämpfe gegen die dämonischen Horden sind anspruchsvoll, aber fair und erfordern strategisches Denken und kluge Planung.

Grafik und Sound:
Die Grafik und der Soundtrack tragen hervorragend zur Atmosphäre bei und verstärken das Gefühl der ständigen Bedrohung und des Überlebenskampfes.

Steuerung und Benutzeroberfläche:
Die Steuerung ist intuitiv und die Benutzeroberfläche übersichtlich, was den Spielspaß zusätzlich erhöht.

Fazit:
Insgesamt kann ich "Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation" jedem Fan von Strategie- und Survival-Spielen wärmstens empfehlen. Die 60 Stunden Spielzeit vergingen wie im Flug, und ich freue mich darauf, noch viele weitere Stunden in dieser faszinierenden Welt zu verbringen.

“The game scores 5-6 out of 10, but it's not bad for an indie developer, especially if he is alone. However, a lot of things are unfinished and underdeveloped, left at the stage of 'oh, we have this too,' making it suitable maximum for only one playthrough.

Mechanics that need improvement:
1.	Allied/Enemy Settlements: Essentially a useless mechanic where it's better not to interact with any settlements beyond being adjacent to you, because the entire mechanic is that a tasks to help this city is added to the pool, and if you don't help, they become enemies and start attacking you (yes, such nonsense, as if the player owes them something and is obliged to help) and it's manageable if they are near your city, but when these cities are on the other side of the map, it's just nonsense. Fortunately, if you don't interact with the cities, they remain "closed." Honestly, without this, I would have given the game 3-4 points, but as it is, you can at least bypass it. Naturally, you have to figure this out yourself or struggle. And I think for such a player, the game would be 3-4 points.
2.	Experience Gain from Battle: My characters at the base are already level 8-10, and my warriors are level 3-5 (and even that is mostly from working at the base while they are healing; otherwise, they would be level 2-3). The distribution of experience to fighters is horrible	.
3.	The Maximum Level Itself: What kind of maximum is 10 levels? Moreover, without indicating it anywhere, I find out about it when I alredy 10 lvl. Also, its completion is at 2.5 upgrades, and why even? It doubles the frustration. It would have been better to finish at 2 or allow upgrading the third branch to full. Also, indicate right away that the max level for a character is 10. It would be better to give characters different level caps altogether; you have a rudimentary rarity mechanic, so you could do the same with characters, like this one up to 10, that one up to 14, and this one up to 16 levels. Or increase the level cap through upgrades and resource gathering. 
4.	Combat Itself: It lacks some depth if you wanted to make it slow. Or control, if you wanted to make it fast, player-controlled. It turned out too bland. And too much dependence on gear..
5.	And the Usual Problem of All Games: The longer you play, the more sluggish the game becomes and its pace slows down. The game should maintain the initial pace or do everything to create the illusion of it. This is not the case here. Initially, you upgrade the base every 5-10 minutes and during that time at least make one sortie to shoot. By day 50, it’s upgrading once every couple of hours of gameplay (real time) and going out to shoot also once every couple of hours (if you are going to gather resources at your development level), 1-3 shootouts with mobs (or even auto-battle, because as I said, there are problems with the engagement of battles) and again you go back to the base to heal fighters, plus debuffs that only wear off after 30-120 minutes of real time, great.
6.	And Outposts: This is also a rather weak mechanic, just a building on the map where you can send 5-7 people to gather the resources available around it. It would have been better to make a full-fledged base, somehow refine/improve the building mechanic to engage players and give players something to do in the mid and late stages of the game (the pace wouldn't drop as much). For example, make it so that to build a building you need not only regular resources but also rare ones, and now the player has something to do (setting up a new base), and this slightly returns the pace to the game (or even make several building levels and these "unusual" resources are needed for their upgrades).
